آخر.etymology: Elative/active-participle formation آخِر (ʾāḫir, 'last, final part; end') from the Semitic root ء-خ-ر (ʾ-ḫ-r, 'to come after, be behind, delay').

آرمة.etymology: Levantine borrowing from Italian arma ('coat of arms, emblem, shop crest'), which came to denote a painted shopfront signboard across the eastern Mediterranean.

history.meaning: coat of arms; emblem; shop sign

آسف.etymology: Active participle آسِف (ʾāsif, 'regretful, sorry') from the verb أَسِفَ (ʾasifa, 'to grieve, feel regret') on the triliteral root ء-س-ف (ʾ-s-f).

آمن.etymology: Active participle آمِن (ʾāmin, 'safe, secure, free from fear') from أَمِنَ (ʾamina, 'to be safe, feel secure'), derived from the Proto-Semitic root ء-م-ن (ʾ-m-n, 'firmness, trust, safety').

آه.etymology: Primary expressive interjection آه (ʾāh), used across Classical and Levantine Arabic as an exclamation of realization ('oh!, ah!') and in Levantine speech as the everyday affirmative ('yes, yeah').

آها.etymology: Expressive exclamation آهَا (ʾāhā, 'aha!, I see!'), an extended emphatic form of آه marking sudden realization or comprehension.

آي.etymology: Natural expressive interjection آي (ʾāy, 'ouch!, ow!') voiced upon sudden pain, heat, or a minor bump.

أبدا.etymology: Adverbial accusative أَبَدًا (ʾabadan, 'ever, forever; [with negation] never, not at all') from the noun أَبَد (ʾabad, 'endless time, eternity'), root ء-ب-د (ʾ-b-d).

أبيض.etymology: Primary colour adjective on the pattern أَفْعَل (afʿal, feminine بَيْضَاء bayḍāʾ > Levantine بيضا) from root ب-ي-ض (b-y-ḍ, 'whiteness, brightness; egg').

أجّر.etymology: Form II verb أَجَّرَ (ʾajjara, 'to rent out, let for hire'), denominative from أَجْر (ʾajr, 'reward, wage, hire') on the Semitic root ء-ج-ر (ʾ-j-r).

history.meaning: to rent out; let on lease

أجّل.etymology: Form II verb أَجَّلَ (ʾajjala, 'to postpone, defer to a later term'), derived from أَجَل (ʾajal, 'appointed time, fixed term') on the root ء-ج-ل (ʾ-j-l).

أحسن.etymology: Elative adjective أَحْسَن (ʾaḥsan, 'better, best') on the comparative pattern أَفْعَل from حَسُنَ (ḥasuna, 'to be good, fine, comely'), root ح-س-ن (ḥ-s-n).

أحلى.etymology: Elative adjective أَحْلَى (ʾaḥlā, 'sweeter, nicest, loveliest') on the pattern أَفْعَل from حَلَا (ḥalā, 'to be sweet, pleasant'), root ح-ل-و (ḥ-l-w).

أحمر.etymology: Primary color adjective أَحْمَر (ʾaḥmar, feminine حَمْرَاء > Levantine حمرا) on the pattern أَفْعَل from the root ح-م-ر (ḥ-m-r, 'redness, ruddy hue').

أحيانا.etymology: Adverbial accusative أَحْيَانًا (ʾaḥyānan, 'at times, sometimes') of أَحْيَان (ʾaḥyān), the broken plural of حِين (ḥīn, 'time, period, moment'), root ح-ي-ن (ḥ-y-n).

أخ.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *'aḫ- ('brother'), one of the core biradical kinship nouns across Semitic languages.
أخ.notes: Before possessive suffixes or in construct, the long stem vowel resurfaces (أخوي 'my brother', أخوك 'your brother'), and the dual is أخوين ('two brothers').

أخد.etymology: Levantine reflex (with regular shift of interdental ذ ḏ to stop د d) of Classical Arabic أَخَذَ (ʾaḫaḏa, 'to take'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʾaḫaḏ-.

أخضر.etymology: Primary colour adjective on the pattern أَفْعَل (afʿal, feminine خَضْرَاء > Levantine خضرا) from Semitic root خ-ض-ر (ḫ-ḍ-r, 'fresh green growth, herbs, vegetables').

أدفى.etymology: Levantine elative أَدْفَى (ʾadfā, 'warmer, warmest') from Classical أَدْفَأ (ʾadfaʾ) via regular loss of final hamza, from the root د-ف-ء (d-f-ʾ, 'warmth, shelter').

أذن.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʾuḏn- ('ear'), a core anatomical noun shared across all branches of Semitic (root ء-ذ-ن).

أربعة.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʾarbaʿ- ('four'), built on the pan-Semitic numeral root ر-ب-ع (r-b-ʿ).

أربعطعش.etymology: Levantine compound numeral contracted from Classical أَرْبَعَةَ عَشَرَ (ʾarbaʿata ʿašara, 'four-teen'), with pharyngeal-triggered emphasis producing the characteristic -ṭaʿš teen suffix.

أربعين.etymology: Oblique/generalized spoken form of Classical أَرْبَعُونَ / أَرْبَعِينَ (ʾarbaʿīna, 'forty'), decade numeral formed with the plural suffix -īn from أَرْبَع (ʾarbaʿ, 'four').

أرز.etymology: Classical Arabic أَرْز (ʾarz, 'cedar tree, cedar wood'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʾarz- ('cedar of Lebanon'), root ء-ر-ز (ʾ-r-z, 'to be firmly rooted').

أرض.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʾarṣ̂- ('earth, land, ground'), one of the most ancient feminine nouns in the Semitic lexicon (root ء-ر-ض).

أرضي.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective أَرْضِيّ (ʾarḍiyy, 'terrestrial, ground-level, ground-floor') derived from أَرْض (ʾarḍ, 'ground, earth') with the suffix -ِيّ (-iyy).

أرضية.etymology: Feminine substantive أَرْضِيَّة (ʾarḍiyya, 'flooring, floor surface, ground base') formed from the relational adjective أَرْضِيّ (ʾarḍiyy).

أرق.etymology: Elative adjective أَرَقّ (ʾaraqq, 'thinner, gentler, more delicate') on the pattern أَفْعَل from the geminate root ر-ق-ق (r-q-q, 'thinness, fineness, tenderness').

أزرق.etymology: Primary colour adjective on the pattern أَفْعَل (afʿal, feminine زَرْقَاء > Levantine زرقا) from root ز-ر-ق (z-r-q, 'clear blue, gleaming sky/water').

أزعج.etymology: Form IV causative verb أَزْعَجَ (ʾazʿaja, 'to unsettle, disturb, bother') from the root ز-ع-ج (z-ʿ-j, 'to disquiet, rouse from rest').

أزمة.etymology: Noun أَزْمَة (ʾazma, 'tightness, strait, crisis') from أَزَمَ (ʾazama, 'to constrict, bite tightly, become severe'); in Jordanian Arabic it also specializes as 'traffic jam, bottleneck'.

أسبوع.etymology: Formed on the pattern أُفْعُول (ʾufʿūl) from the numeral root س-ب-ع (s-b-ʿ, 'seven'), naming the seven-day week.

أستاذ.etymology: Classical Arabic أُسْتَاذ (ʾustāḏ, 'master craftsman, teacher, tutor; polite title sir/Mr'), borrowed from Middle Persian awestād ('master, skilled artisan').

أسوأ.etymology: Elative adjective أَسْوَأ (ʾaswaʾ, 'worse, worst') on the pattern أَفْعَل from سَاءَ (sāʾa, 'to be bad, evil'), root س-و-ء (s-w-ʾ).

أسود.etymology: Formed on the colour/defect elative pattern أَفْعَل (afʿal, feminine فَعْلَاء sawdāʾ > Levantine سودا) from root س-و-د (s-w-d, 'black, dark').

أشرف.etymology: Form IV verb أَشْرَفَ (ʾašrafa, 'to look down from an elevation; oversee, supervise') from شَرَف (šaraf, 'high ground, eminence'), root ش-ر-ف (š-r-f).

أشّر.etymology: Form II verb أَشَّرَ (ʾaššara, 'to make a sign, point, wave, mark') from the root ء-ش-ر (ʾ-š-r, 'marking, pointing, gesturing').

أصبح.etymology: Form IV verb أَصْبَحَ (ʾaṣbaḥa, 'to enter upon the morning; wake at dawn; become') derived from صُبْح (ṣubḥ, 'morning, daybreak'), root ص-ب-ح (ṣ-b-ḥ).

history.meaning: to enter morning; wake in the morning; become

أصغر.etymology: Elative adjective أَصْغَر (ʾaṣġar, 'smaller, smallest; younger, youngest') on the pattern أَفْعَل from صَغُرَ (ṣaġura, 'to be small'), root ص-غ-ر (ṣ-ġ-r).

أصفر.etymology: Primary colour adjective on the pattern أَفْعَل (afʿal, feminine صَفْرَاء > Levantine صفرا) from root ص-ف-ر (ṣ-f-r, 'yellow, golden-pale, gleaming brass').

أصلا.etymology: Adverbial accusative أَصْلًا (ʾaṣlan, 'originally, fundamentally, in the first place') from أَصْل (ʾaṣl, 'root, foundation, origin'), root ء-ص-ل (ʾ-ṣ-l).

history.meaning: at root; originally; in the first place

أصلي.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective أَصْلِيّ (ʾaṣliyy, 'original, authentic, genuine') formed from أَصْل (ʾaṣl, 'root, origin') + -ِيّ (-iyy), root ء-ص-ل.

أصيل.etymology: Adjective أَصِيل ('genuine, authentic, deep-rooted') on the pattern فَعِيل from أَصْل ('root, origin, foundation', root ء-ص-ل): literally 'firmly rooted in its true nature'.

أطول.etymology: Elative adjective أَطْوَل (ʾaṭwal, 'taller, longest, longer') on the pattern أَفْعَل from طَالَ (ṭāla, 'to be long, tall'), root ط-و-ل (ṭ-w-l).

أعطى.etymology: Form IV verb أَعْطَى (ʾaʿṭā, 'to give, grant, hand over') from the root ع-ط-و (ʿ-ṭ-w, 'to reach for, take in the hand, offer').

أغرب.etymology: Elative adjective أَغْرَب (ʾaġrab, 'stranger, strangest') on the pattern أَفْعَل from غَرِيب (ġarīb, 'strange, unfamiliar, foreign'), root غ-ر-ب (ġ-r-b).

أغلب.etymology: Elative adjective أَغْلَب (ʾaġlab, 'predominant, most, majority') on the pattern أَفْعَل from غَلَبَ (ġalaba, 'to prevail, overcome'), root غ-ل-ب (ġ-l-b).

أغنية.etymology: Derived on the pattern أُفْعولة (ufʿūla) from the root غ-ن-ي (gh-n-y), whose Form II verb غَنَّى (ghannā) means 'to sing, chant melodiously'.

أقل.etymology: Elative adjective أَقَلّ (ʾaqall, 'less, fewer, least') on the pattern أَفْعَل from the geminate root ق-ل-ل (q-l-l, 'to be few, small in quantity').

أكتر.etymology: Levantine reflex (with regular shift of interdental ث ṯ to stop ت t) of Classical Arabic أَكْثَر (ʾakṯar, 'more, most'), elative of كَثِير (kaṯīr, 'many, much'), root ك-ث-ر.

أكل.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʾakal- ('to eat, consume'), one of the most conserved primary verbs across all Semitic languages (root ء-ك-ل).

أكيد.etymology: Adjective and adverb أَكِيد (ʾakīd, 'certain, sure; definitely') on the pattern فَعِيل from the root ء-ك-د (ʾ-k-d, 'to fasten, confirm, make firm').

ألقى.etymology: Form IV verb أَلْقَى (ʾalqā, 'to cast, throw, direct [a glance or speech]') from the root ل-ق-ي (l-q-y, 'to meet, encounter, place before').

ألو.etymology: Standard telephone greeting أَلُو (ʾalō), borrowed via French allô from English hallo / hello in the late 19th-century spread of telephony.

أم.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʾimm- ('mother'), an ancient nursery and kinship noun universal across the Semitic family (root ء-م-م).

أمامي.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective أَمَامِيّ (ʾamāmiyy, 'front, forward, anterior') formed from أَمَام (ʾamāma, 'in front of'), root ء-م-م (ʾ-m-m, 'to go before, lead').

أمان.etymology: Verbal/abstract noun أَمَان (ʾamān, 'safety, security, protection, peace of mind') from أَمِنَ (ʾamina, 'to be safe'), root ء-م-ن (ʾ-m-n).

أمانة.etymology: Noun أَمَانَة (ʾamāna, 'trustworthiness; something entrusted for safekeeping; civic municipality') from أَمُنَ (ʾamuna, 'to be faithful, trustworthy'), root ء-م-ن.

history.meaning: trust; deposit held in safekeeping; stewardship

أمر.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʾamār- ('to say, command, make known'), yielding Classical Arabic أَمْر (ʾamr, 'command, order; matter, affair'), root ء-م-ر.

أنا.etymology: First-person singular independent pronoun أَنَا (ʾanā, 'I'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʾanā (alongside *ʾanāku).

أنف.etymology: Ancient Proto-Semitic body-part noun أَنْف ('nose; proud promontory') from `*ʾanp-`, preserving the original medial `-n-` that assimilated to `-pp-` in Northwest Semitic.

أنقذ.etymology: Form IV causative verb أَنْقَذَ (ʾanqaḏa, 'to rescue, save, deliver from danger') from نَقَذَ (naqaḏa, 'to escape, be safe'), root ن-ق-ذ (n-q-ḏ).

أهدى.etymology: Levantine elative أَهْدَى (ʾahdā, 'quieter, calmer, calmest') from Classical أَهْدَأ (ʾahdaʾ) via regular loss of final glottal stop, from هَدَأَ (hadaʾa, 'to be calm, quiet'), root ه-د-ء.

أهلا.etymology: Accusative greeting أَهْلًا (ʾahlan, 'welcome!, hello!'), elliptically shortened from the classical hospitality formula حَلَلْتَ أَهْلًا وَنَزَلْتَ سَهْلًا ('you have come among family and stepped onto smooth ground'), from أَهْل ('family, kin', root ء-ه-ل).

أو.etymology: Coordinating conjunction أَوْ (ʾaw, 'or'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʾaw ('or').

أوبس.etymology: Modern conversational interjection borrowed from English oops!, used playfully after a minor slip or spill.

history.meaning: exclamation after a small mistake or spill

أوف.etymology: Expressive exclamation أُوف (ʾūf, 'oof!, ugh!, phew!') voicing fatigue, relief, or dismay; closely related to the Classical interjection أُفّ (ʾuff, 'fie!, ugh!').

أوكتاف.etymology: Musical terminology loanword borrowed from French octave ('interval of eight diatonic degrees'), from Latin octāva ('eighth').

history.meaning: musical interval of eight scale steps

أول.etymology: Elative-pattern ordinal أَوَّل (ʾawwal, 'first, foremost, beginning'), derived from the root أ-و-ل / و-أ-ل ('to precede, be foremost; return to origin').

أوه.etymology: Natural expressive exclamation أُوه (ʾōh, 'oh!') marking mild surprise, sympathy, or sudden realization.

أي.etymology: Interrogative and indefinite determiner أَيّ (ʾayy, 'which?; any'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʾayy- ('which, where').

أيار.etymology: Levantine month name أَيَّار (ʾAyyār, 'May'), borrowed through Aramaic/Syriac ܐܝܪ (ʾīyār) from Akkadian Ayyaru ('blossom, rosette; second month of the Babylonian spring calendar').

أيمتى.etymology: Levantine interrogative adverb أَيْمَتَى / إِيمْتَى (ʾēmtā, 'when?'), compounded from أَيّ (ʾayy, 'which [time]') + مَتَى (matā, 'when?', from Proto-Semitic *matay).

أيوا.etymology: Warm Levantine and Egyptian affirmative particle أَيْوَا / أَيْوَه (ʾaywa, 'yes!, that\'s right!'), contracted from the Classical oath phrase أَيْ وَاللّٰهِ (ʾay wallāhi, 'yes, by God!').

إبريق.etymology: Early borrowing into Classical Arabic from Middle Persian *ābrēz / ābrēg* ('water-pourer', from *āb* 'water' + *rēxtan* 'to pour').
إبريق.notes: Names a spouted teapot, kettle, or pitcher (plural أباريق).

إبط.etymology: Classical Arabic anatomical noun إِبْط (ʾibṭ, 'armpit, underarm'), from the Semitic root ء-ب-ط (ʾ-b-ṭ).

إجا.etymology: Levantine verb إِجَا (ʾijā, 'to come'), reshaped from Classical Arabic جَاءَ (jāʾa, root ج-ي-ء) by loss of final hamza and addition of a prosthetic initial vowel on analogy with weak-final verbs.

إحنا.etymology: Spoken Levantine first-person plural pronoun إِحْنَا (ʾiḥnā, 'we'), developed from Classical Arabic نَحْنُ (naḥnu, Proto-Semitic *niḥnū / *ʾanḥnū) with loss of initial n- and generalized -nā ending.

إذا.etymology: Conditional and temporal conjunction إِذَا (ʾiḏā, 'when, if'), built on the Proto-Semitic demonstrative/temporal base *ʾiḏ- ('then, when').

إذن.etymology: Verbal noun إِذْن (ʾiḏn, 'permission, leave, authorization') from أَذِنَ (ʾaḏina, 'to give ear, listen to, allow'), derived from the Semitic ear/hearing root ء-ذ-ن (ʾ-ḏ-n).

إزعاج.etymology: Form IV verbal noun (maṣdar) إِزْعَاج (ʾizʿāj, 'disturbance, bother, annoyance') of أَزْعَجَ (ʾazʿaja, 'to disturb, unsettle'), root ز-ع-ج (z-ʿ-j).

إسفنجة.etymology: Singulative noun إِسْفَنْجَة ('a sponge') from collective إِسْفَنْج, borrowed in antiquity from Greek σπόγγος / σφόγγος ('sea sponge')—the same Mediterranean source behind English 'sponge'.

cognates.meaning: cleaning sponge, from the same Greek source

إشعار.etymology: Form IV verbal noun إِشْعَار (ʾišʿār, 'notification, notice, making known') from أَشْعَرَ (ʾašʿara, 'to inform, notify'), root ش-ع-ر (š-ʿ-r, 'to perceive, feel, know').

إشي.etymology: Jordanian and Palestinian spoken noun إِشِي (ʾiši, 'thing, something, anything'), evolved from Classical شَيْء (šayʾ, 'thing', root ش-ي-ء) with a prosthetic vowel and reinforced by the interrogative phrase أَيُّ شَيْءٍ ('what thing? / anything').

إصبع.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʾiṣbaʿ- ('finger, toe'), preserved in Classical Arabic as إِصْبَع (ʾiṣbaʿ), root ص-ب-ع (ṣ-b-ʿ).

إطلالة.etymology: Form IV instance/verbal noun إِطْلَالَة (ʾiṭlāla, 'overlook, scenic view, appearance from above') from أَطَلَّ (ʾaṭalla, 'to look down upon, overlook'), root ط-ل-ل (ṭ-l-l).

history.meaning: looking out from above; view; outlook

إلا.etymology: Compound exception particle إِلَّا (ʾillā, 'except, unless; [in time-telling] minutes to the hour'), formed from conditional إِنْ (ʾin, 'if') + negative لَا (lā, 'not').

إلى.etymology: Directional preposition إِلَى (ʾilā, 'to, toward, until'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʾilay ('toward, unto').

إم.etymology: Spoken Levantine form إِمّ (ʾimm, 'mother, mum') with characteristic high front vowel i, preserving the Proto-Semitic vocalism *ʾimm- alongside Classical Arabic أُمّ (ʾumm).

إن.etymology: Classical and Levantine particle covering both conditional إِنْ (ʾin, 'if', as in إِنْ شَاءَ اللّٰهُ 'God willing') and the complementizer إِنَّ / أَنَّ ('that, indeed'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʾin / *ʾanna.

إنت.etymology: Spoken Levantine second-person masculine singular pronoun إِنْتَ / إِنْت (ʾinta / ʾint, 'you'), from Classical Arabic أَنْتَ (ʾanta), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʾanta.

إنتو.etymology: Spoken Levantine second-person plural pronoun إِنْتُو (ʾintū, 'you all'), evolved from Classical Arabic أَنْتُمْ (ʾantum, Proto-Semitic *ʾantum) with shift of the plural ending -um to -ū.

إنتي.etymology: Spoken Levantine second-person feminine singular pronoun إِنْتِي (ʾintī, 'you'), from Classical أَنْتِ (ʾanti), retaining the Proto-Semitic long final vowel *ʾantī.

إي.etymology: Classical and Levantine affirmative particle إِي (ʾī, 'yes, yea, indeed'), attested in Classical Arabic before oaths (إِي وَرَبِّي 'yes, by my Lord') and used standalone in everyday Levantine speech.

إياه.etymology: Detached direct-object pronoun إِيَّاهُ (ʾiyyāhu, 'him, it'), composed of the pronominal object base إِيَّا- (ʾiyyā-) + third-person masculine singular suffix -هُ (-hu).

إيجار.etymology: Form IV verbal noun إِيجَار (ʾījār < *ʾiʾjār, 'rent, lease, letting out') from آجَرَ (ʾājara, 'to let for hire'), root ء-ج-ر (ʾ-j-r).

إيد.etymology: Spoken Levantine noun إِيد (ʾīd, 'hand, handle'), reshaped with a long stem vowel from Classical Arabic يَد (yad, Proto-Semitic *yad-) by leveling from the dual/broken-plural stem أَيْدٍ (ʾaydin).

إيقاع.etymology: Form IV verbal noun إِيقَاع ('rhythm, cadence') from the root و-ق-ع ('fall, land in beats'): literally 'letting beats fall in measured time', established since al-Kindi and al-Farabi as the core Arabic term for musical rhythm.

إيمتى.etymology: Levantine interrogative adverb إِيمْتَى (ʾēmtā, 'when?'), compounded from أَيّ (ʾayy, 'which [time]') + مَتَى (matā, 'when?', from Proto-Semitic *matay).

ابتسم.etymology: Form VIII verb اِبْتَسَمَ (ibtasama, 'to smile') from بَسَمَ (basama, 'to part the lips in a gentle smile'), root ب-س-م (b-s-m).

ابن.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *bin- ('son'), with a prosthetic vowel in Classical Arabic اِبْن (ibn), root ب-ن-ي (b-n-y, 'to build').

اتصل.etymology: Form VIII verb اِتَّصَلَ (ittaṣala < *iwtaṣala, 'to be joined, connected; get in touch, telephone') with assimilation of initial w- to -t-, from وَصَلَ (waṣala, 'to join, arrive'), root و-ص-ل.

اتفق.etymology: Form VIII verb اِتَّفَقَ (ittafaqa < *iwtafaqa, 'to agree, concur, come to an accord') from وَفِقَ (wafiqa, 'to be fitting, harmonious'), root و-ف-ق (w-f-q).

history.meaning: to agree; come to an agreement

اتنعش.etymology: Spoken Levantine compound numeral اِتْنَعْش (itnaʿš, 'twelve'), contracted from Classical اِثْنَا عَشَرَ (iṯnā ʿašara, 'two-teen') with regular shift of interdental ṯ to t.

احتاج.etymology: Form VIII verb (افتعل) from the root ح-و-ج (h-w-j), associated with need, want, and necessity.
احتاج.notes: In everyday Jordanian conversation, speakers often use the active participle محتاج ('needing, in need of') alongside بده.

احترم.etymology: Form VIII verb اِحْتَرَمَ (iḥtarama, 'to revere, honor, respect') derived from the Semitic root ح-ر-م (ḥ-r-m, 'sacredness, inviolability').

احتفل.etymology: Form VIII verb اِحْتَفَلَ (iḥtafala, 'to gather in a festive crowd, celebrate') from حَفَلَ (ḥafala, 'to assemble, teem'), root ح-ف-ل (ḥ-f-l).

history.meaning: to assemble in a crowd; celebrate

احتياط.etymology: Form VIII verbal noun اِحْتِيَاط (iḥtiyāṭ, 'precaution, safeguard; reserve, spare item') from اِحْتَاطَ (iḥtāṭa, 'to surround, guard, take precaution'), root ح-و-ط (ḥ-w-ṭ).

اختار.etymology: Form VIII verb اِخْتَارَ (iḫtāra, 'to choose, select, prefer') derived from خَيْر (ḫayr, 'good, best'), root خ-ي-ر (ḫ-y-r).

اختيار.etymology: Form VIII verbal noun اِخْتِيَار (iḫtiyār, 'choice, selection, free will') of اِخْتَارَ (iḫtāra, 'to choose'), root خ-ي-ر (ḫ-y-r).

ارتاح.etymology: Form VIII verb اِرْتَاحَ (irtāḥa, 'to rest, relax, feel at ease') from رَاحَة (rāḥa, 'rest, ease, relief'), root ر-و-ح (r-w-ḥ, 'breeze, breath, repose').

ارتبك.etymology: Form VIII mediopassive verb اِرْتَبَكَ (irtabaka, 'to become entangled, confused, flustered') from رَبَكَ (rabaka, 'to mix, entangle'), root ر-ب-ك (r-b-k).

history.meaning: to become entangled; get flustered or confused

ارتعب.etymology: Form VIII mediopassive verb اِرْتَعَبَ (irtaʿaba, 'to be terrified, startled, panic') from رَعَبَ (raʿaba, 'to frighten, fill with dread'), root ر-ع-ب (r-ʿ-b).

history.meaning: to be frightened; panic; be startled

ارتفع.etymology: Form VIII mediopassive verb اِرْتَفَعَ (irtafaʿa, 'to rise, ascend, increase in height or level') from رَفَعَ (rafaʿa, 'to lift, raise'), root ر-ف-ع (r-f-ʿ).

history.meaning: to rise; be raised; go up

استأهل.etymology: Form X verb اِسْتَأْهَلَ (istaʾhala > spoken Levantine بستاهل bistāhal, 'to deserve, be worthy of'), denominative from أَهْل (ʾahl, 'worthy, fit for; family'), root ء-ه-ل.

history.meaning: to merit; be worthy of; deserve

استعجل.etymology: Form X verb اِسْتَعْجَلَ (istaʿjala, 'to hurry, rush, seek haste') from عَجِلَ (ʿajila, 'to hasten, be quick'), root ع-ج-ل (ʿ-j-l).

استعمل.etymology: Form X verb اِسْتَعْمَلَ (istaʿmala, 'to put to work, use, employ') from عَمِلَ (ʿamila, 'to work, make, do'), root ع-م-ل (ʿ-m-l).

history.meaning: to use; employ; put to work

استقبال.etymology: Form X verbal noun اِسْتِقْبَال (istiqbāl, 'going forward to meet; reception, welcome; front desk') from اِسْتَقْبَلَ (istaqbala), root ق-ب-ل (q-b-l).

استقبل.etymology: Form X verb اِسْتَقْبَلَ (istaqbala, 'to face, go to meet, welcome, receive guests') from the Semitic root ق-ب-ل (q-b-l, 'front; facing; accepting').

استلم.etymology: Form VIII verb اِسْتَلَمَ (istalama, 'to receive, take delivery of, take over a post'), originally in Classical Arabic 'to touch or greet the stone (سِلْم)' from root س-ل-م (s-l-m).

history.meaning: to touch; receive in hand; take charge of

استنى.etymology: Spoken Levantine and Egyptian verb اِسْتَنَّى (istannā, 'to wait'), evolved by assimilation of the glottal stop from Classical Form X اِسْتَأْنَى (istaʾnā, 'to wait patiently, take one\'s time'), root ء-ن-ي (ʾ-n-y).

history.meaning: to wait patiently; bide one's time

اسم.etymology: An ancient Proto-Semitic basic noun (*šim- 'name'), written in Arabic with an initial prosthetic vowel (همزة الوصل) before the two root consonants س-م.
اسم.notes: Cognates appear across every branch of Semitic, making اسم one of the oldest everyday words in Arabic.

اشتاق.etymology: Form VIII verb اِشْتَاقَ (ištāqa, 'to yearn, long for, miss someone') from شَوْق (šawq, 'longing, yearning'), root ش-و-ق (š-w-q).

اشترى.etymology: Form VIII verb اِشْتَرَى (ištarā, 'to buy, purchase') from شَرَى (šarā, 'to trade, exchange, buy/sell'), root ش-ر-ي (š-r-y).

اشتغل.etymology: Form VIII verb اِشْتَغَلَ (ištaġala, 'to be busy, work, run/operate') from شُغْل (šuġl, 'work, occupation'), root ش-غ-ل (š-ġ-l).

اضطر.etymology: Form VIII verb اِضْطَرَّ (iḍṭarra, 'to compel; [in passive/spoken] be forced, have to'), where the Form VIII infix -t- assimilates in emphasis to -ṭ- after root-initial ض (ḍ), from root ض-ر-ر (ḍ-r-r, 'necessity, pressure').

history.meaning: to compel; be forced or obliged to

اطمن.etymology: Spoken Levantine verb اِطَّمَّن (iṭṭamman, 'to feel reassured, check on someone'), reshaped from Classical quadriliteral Form IV اِطْمَأَنَّ (iṭmaʾanna, 'to be tranquil, calm, reassured'), root ط-م-أ-ن.

اطنعش.etymology: Spoken Levantine compound numeral اِطْنَعْش (iṭnaʿš, 'twelve'), contracted from Classical اِثْنَا عَشَرَ (iṯnā ʿašara, 'two-teen') with emphatic ṭ induced by pharyngeal ʿayn.

اعتذر.etymology: Form VIII verb اِعْتَذَرَ (iʿtaḏara, 'to offer an excuse, apologize') from عُذْر (ʿuḏr, 'excuse, pardon'), root ع-ذ-ر (ʿ-ḏ-r).

اعتمد.etymology: Form VIII verb اِعْتَمَدَ (iʿtamada, 'to lean upon, rely on, count on') from عَمَدَ (ʿamada, 'to support, prop up with a pillar [عَمُود]'), root ع-م-د (ʿ-m-d).

history.meaning: to lean upon; rely on; depend on

افتتاح.etymology: Form VIII verbal noun اِفْتِتَاح (iftitāḥ, 'inauguration, grand opening, commencement') from اِفْتَتَحَ (iftataḥa, 'to open ceremonially'), root ف-ت-ح (f-t-ḥ).

الأحد.etymology: Short for يَوْم الأَحَد ('day one / the first day'), built from the Semitic numeral root ء-ح-د ('one') on the stem أَحَد. Alongside الإثنين ('Monday, day two'), الثلاثاء ('Tuesday, day three'), الأربعاء ('Wednesday, day four'), and الخميس ('Thursday, day five'), it preserves the ancient Near Eastern numbered-day week.

الأربعا.etymology: Spoken Levantine form of يَوْم الْأَرْبِعَاء (yawm al-ʾarbiʿāʾ, 'the fourth day'), derived from the Semitic numeral root ر-ب-ع (r-b-ʿ, 'four').

التلاتا.etymology: Spoken Levantine reflex (with regular shift of ṯ to t and loss of final hamza) of Classical يَوْمُ الثُّلَاثَاءِ (al-ṯulāṯāʾ, 'Tuesday', literally 'the third day [of the week]'), root ث-ل-ث (ṯ-l-ṯ, 'three').

التنين.etymology: Spoken Levantine reflex (with regular shift of ṯ to t) of Classical يَوْمُ الِاثْنَيْنِ (al-iṯnayn, 'Monday', literally 'the second day [of the week]'), from اِثْنَانِ ('two', root ث-ن-ي).

الجمعة.etymology: Classical and Levantine يَوْمُ الجُمُعَةِ (al-jumʿa, 'Friday', literally 'the day of congregational gathering'), from the root ج-م-ع (j-m-ʿ, 'to gather, assemble').

الخميس.etymology: Short for يَوْم الْخَمِيس (yawm al-ḫamīs, 'the fifth day'), built on pattern فَعِيل from the Semitic numeral root خ-م-س (ḫ-m-s, 'five').

السبت.etymology: From Classical Arabic السَّبْت (as-sabt, 'Saturday, Sabbath'), from Semitic root س-ب-ت (s-b-t, 'to rest, cease work at week's end'), cognate with Hebrew Šabbāṯ and Aramaic Šabbəṯā.

اللي.etymology: Spoken Arabic invariant relative pronoun اِلِّي (illī, 'who, which, that'), evolved by phonetic reduction and leveling from Classical Arabic الَّذِي / الَّتِي / الَّذِينَ (allaḏī / allatī / allaḏīna).

انتبه.etymology: Form VIII verb اِنْتَبَهَ (intabaha, 'to wake up, become alert, notice, pay attention') from نَبِهَ (nabiha, 'to be perceptive, awake'), root ن-ب-ه (n-b-h).

history.meaning: to become alert; pay attention; watch out

انتهى.etymology: Form VIII mediopassive verb اِنْتَهَى (intahā, 'to reach the end, come to a close, be finished') from نَهَى (nahā, 'to reach a limit; forbid'), root ن-ه-ي (n-h-y).

history.meaning: to reach an end; finish; conclude

انحط.etymology: Form VII passive/intransitive verb اِنْحَطَّ (inḥaṭṭa, 'to be put down, be placed, descend') from حَطَّ (ḥaṭṭa, 'to put down, set down'), root ح-ط-ط (ḥ-ṭ-ṭ).

history.meaning: to be set down; be placed

اندفع.etymology: Form VII verb اِنْدَفَعَ (indafaʿa, 'to rush forward; [in Levantine] to be paid') formed with the detransitivizing prefix in- from دَفَعَ (dafaʿa, 'to push; pay'), root د-ف-ع (d-f-ʿ).

history.meaning: to be pushed forward; be paid

انسحب.etymology: Form VII mediopassive verb اِنْسَحَبَ (insaḥaba, 'to be pulled back, withdraw, retreat') from سَحَبَ (saḥaba, 'to pull, drag, draw'), root س-ح-ب (s-ḥ-b).

انفتح.etymology: Form VII anticausative/passive verb اِنْفَتَحَ (infataḥa, 'to come open, be opened') from فَتَحَ (fataḥa, 'to open'), root ف-ت-ح (f-t-ḥ).

history.meaning: to open by itself; be opened

انقطع.etymology: Form VII mediopassive verb اِنْقَطَعَ (inqaṭaʿa, 'to be cut off, snap, be interrupted') from قَطَعَ (qaṭaʿa, 'to cut, sever'), root ق-ط-ع (q-ṭ-ʿ).

history.meaning: to be cut off; snap; cease

انكتب.etymology: Form VII passive verb اِنْكَتَبَ (inkataba, 'to be written, get inscribed') from كَتَبَ (kataba, 'to write'), root ك-ت-ب (k-t-b).

انكسر.etymology: Form VII anticausative/passive verb اِنْكَسَرَ (inkasara, 'to break, snap, shatter') from كَسَرَ (kasara, 'to break'), root ك-س-ر (k-s-r).

انلف.etymology: Levantine Form VII passive verb اِنْلَفّ (inlaff, 'to be wrapped, get packed or rolled') from لَفَّ (laffa, 'to wrap, fold, turn'), root ل-ف-ف (l-f-f).

انمزع.etymology: Levantine Form VII anticausative/passive verb اِنْمَزَع (inmazaʿ, 'to tear, get ripped') from مَزَعَ (mazaʿa, 'to tear, pluck, rend'), root م-ز-ع (m-z-ʿ).

اهتم.etymology: Form VIII verb اِهْتَمَّ (ihtamma, 'to be concerned, take care of, pay heed to') from هَمَّ (hamma, 'to concern, occupy the mind'), root ه-م-م (h-m-m).

history.meaning: to be concerned; care for; look after

ب.etymology: Inseparable proclitic preposition بِـ (bi-, 'in, at, with, by'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *bi- ('in, with, by').

باب.etymology: An ancient Semitic word for 'door, gate, entrance' (already attested in Akkadian *bābu* and Aramaic *bābā*).
باب.notes: Yields the derived feminine noun بوابة ('outer gate, portal') for the iron courtyard entrance.

بابونج.etymology: Classical Arabic botanical and medical term بَابُونَج ('chamomile'), borrowed during the Abbasid pharmacological era from Middle Persian bābūnag (modern Persian بابونه bābūneh) and treasured across Levantine households as a calming evening tea.

بارد.etymology: Active participle adjective بَارِد (bārid, 'cold, cool, chilly') from بَرَدَ (barada, 'to be cold'), root ب-ر-د (b-r-d).

بارك.etymology: Form III verb بَارَكَ (bāraka, 'to bless, invoke blessing upon; congratulate'), derived from the Semitic root ب-ر-ك (b-r-k, 'blessing; kneeling').

باص.etymology: Modern transport loanword borrowed from English bus (itself clipped from Latin omnibus, 'for all').

باع.etymology: Hollow Form I verb بَاعَ (bāʿa, 'to sell, strike a bargain') from the root ب-ي-ع (b-y-ʿ), originally referring to stretching out the arm (بَاع) to clasp hands when sealing a commercial transaction.

باقي.etymology: Active participle بَاقٍ / البَاقِي (bāqī, 'remaining; the rest, the remainder, monetary change') from بَقِيَ (baqiya, 'to remain, stay'), root ب-ق-ي (b-q-y).

بال.etymology: Classical and Levantine noun بَال (bāl, 'mind, attention, heart, state'), used in core idioms such as دير بالك ('take care') and طول بالك ('be patient'), root ب-و-ل (b-w-l).

بالزبط.etymology: Spoken Levantine adverb بِالزَّبْط (bi-z-zabṭ, 'exactly, spot-on'), reflecting the urban/sibilant pronunciation of Classical بِالضَّبْطِ (bi-l-ḍabṭ, 'with precision'), from ضَبَطَ ('to hold fast, regulate accurately', root ض-ب-ط).

ببلاش.etymology: Levantine and Egyptian adverb بِبَلَاش (bi-balāš, 'for free, at no cost'), contracted from بِـ (bi-, 'with/for') + بِلَا شَيْءٍ (bilā šayʾin, 'without anything, for nothing').

بجعة.etymology: Singulative noun بَجَعَة (bajaʿa, 'swan; pelican') formed with the suffix -ة (-a) from the Classical collective بَجَع (bajaʿ, 'pelicans, large waterbirds'), root ب-ج-ع (b-j-ʿ).

بحر.etymology: Classical Arabic noun بَحْر ('sea, great river', plural بِحَار / بُحُور) from the Semitic root ب-ح-ر ('wide cleft expanse of water'), used metaphorically in classical poetry for boundless generosity and for poetic meters.

بدأ.etymology: Form I verb بَدَأَ (badaʾa, 'to begin, start, originate'), from the Semitic root ب-د-ء (b-d-ʾ, 'beginning, first doing').

بداية.etymology: Noun بِدَايَة ('beginning, opening') from the root ب-د-ء / ب-د-ي ('begin, start first'), paired naturally with نِهَايَة ('ending').

بدل.etymology: Noun and preposition بَدَل (badal, 'substitute, replacement; instead of, in place of') from بَدَلَ (badala, 'to exchange, replace'), root ب-د-ل (b-d-l).

بده.etymology: Signature Levantine volitional pseudo-verb بِدُّه (biddo, 'he wants, needs'; 1sg بِدِّي biddī), grammaticalized and contracted from Classical Arabic بِوُدِّهِ (bi-wuddihi, 'in his wish/desire'), from وُدّ ('love, wish, desire', root و-د-د).

history.meaning: in his wish; by his desire

بدون.etymology: Compound preposition بِدُونِ (bi-dūni, 'without'), formed from the preposition بِـ (bi-) + دُونَ (dūna, 'short of, below, without'), root د-و-ن (d-w-n).

برا.etymology: Spoken Levantine adverb and preposition بَرَّا (barrā, 'outside, out of doors'), from Classical بَرًّا ('on open land') reinforced by Aramaic בָּרָא / ܒܪܐ (bārā, 'open country, outside'), from Semitic root ب-ر-ر (b-r-r, 'open land').

برتقال.etymology: Collective noun بُرْتُقَال (burtuqāl, 'sweet oranges'), borrowed via Ottoman Turkish portakal and Italian portogallo after the country Portugal, whose maritime traders popularized sweet Chinese oranges across the Mediterranean.

برج.etymology: Classical Arabic بُرْج (burj, 'tower, fortress turret, constellation'), borrowed in late antiquity via Aramaic from Byzantine Greek πύργος (púrgos) / Late Latin burgus ('watchtower, castellum').

برد.etymology: Form I verb بَرَدَ (barada, 'to become cold, cool down'), inherited from the Semitic root ب-ر-د (b-r-d, 'coldness, hail, cooling').

برغي.etymology: Levantine and Iraqi noun بُرْغِي (burġī, 'screw, bolt'), borrowed from Ottoman Turkish burgu ('auger, gimlet, screw', derived from the Turkic verb bur- 'to twist, bore').

برق.etymology: Inherited Proto-Semitic noun بَرْق ('lightning') from the root ب-ر-ق ('flash, gleam, shine brightly').

بريد.etymology: Classical Arabic بَرِيد (barīd, 'postal courier, mail service'), borrowed in antiquity via Syriac/Middle Persian from Late Latin verēdus / Byzantine Greek βέρηδος ('post-horse, state relay horse').

بس.etymology: Spoken Levantine, Egyptian, and Gulf particle بَسّ (bass, 'only, just; enough!; but'), borrowed from Persian بَس (bas, 'enough, sufficient, only').

بسطة.etymology: Noun بَسْطَة (basṭa, 'flat expanse, stair landing; open vendor stall') from بَسَطَ (basaṭa, 'to spread out flat'), root ب-س-ط (b-s-ṭ).

history.meaning: spread-out surface; stair landing; market stall

بسكوت.etymology: Collective noun بَسْكُوت (baskūt, 'biscuits, cookies'), borrowed via Italian biscotto ('twice-baked crisp bread/cookie', from Latin bis coctus).

بسيط.etymology: Adjective بَسِيط (basīṭ, 'spread out, uncompounded, simple, minor') on the pattern فَعِيل from بَسَطَ (basaṭa, 'to spread out flat, make plain'), root ب-س-ط (b-s-ṭ).

بطاقة.etymology: Classical Arabic بِطَاقَة (biṭāqa, 'small slip of paper tied to a garment or bale; label, tag, card'), borrowed from Koine Greek πιττάκιον (pittákion, 'writing tablet, label, note').

بطال.etymology: Intensive adjective بَطَّال (baṭṭāl, 'idle, worthless, bad; [in Levantine مش بطال] not bad!') on the pattern فَعَّال from بَطَلَ (baṭala, 'to become null, idle, vain'), root ب-ط-ل (b-ط-l).

بطانة.etymology: Noun بِطَانَة (biṭāna, 'inner lining of a coat or mechanism; felt bushing') derived from بَطْن (baṭn, 'interior, inside, belly'), root ب-ط-ن (b-ṭ-n).

بطلة.etymology: Feminine noun بَطَلَة (baṭala, 'heroine, female champion') from بَطَل (baṭal, 'hero, brave warrior, champion') on the root ب-ط-ل (b-ṭ-l, 'valor, bravery').

بطيء.etymology: Adjective بَطِيء (baṭīʾ, 'slow, tardy, unhurried') on the pattern فَعِيل from بَطُؤَ (baṭuʾa, 'to be slow'), root ب-ط-ء (b-ṭ-ʾ).

بطّل.etymology: Form II verb بَطَّلَ (baṭṭala, 'to invalidate, cease, stop doing something') from بَطَلَ (baṭala, 'to become void, cease'), root ب-ط-ل (b-ṭ-l).

بعت.etymology: Spoken Levantine reflex (with regular shift of interdental ث ṯ to dental stop ت t) of Classical Arabic بَعَثَ (baʿaṯa, 'to send, dispatch'), root ب-ع-ث (b-ʿ-ṯ).

بعد.etymology: Preposition and adverb بَعْدَ (baʿda, 'after, later, still'), inherited from the Proto-Semitic spatial/temporal root ب-ع-د (b-ʿ-d, 'distance, behind, after').

بعدين.etymology: Spoken Levantine temporal adverb بَعْدِين (baʿdēn, 'then, afterwards, later'), formed as an adverbial dual/extension from بَعْد (baʿd, 'after'), root ب-ع-د.

بعض.etymology: Noun and reciprocal pronoun بَعْض (baʿḍ, 'part, portion, some; [after plural verbs] each other, one another'), from the root ب-ع-ض (b-ʿ-ḍ, 'to divide into parts').

بعيد.etymology: Adjective بَعِيد (baʿīd, 'far, distant, remote') on the pattern فَعِيل from بَعُدَ (baʿuda, 'to be distant'), root ب-ع-د (b-ʿ-d).

بكرا.etymology: Spoken Levantine and Egyptian temporal adverb بُكْرَا (bukrā, 'tomorrow'), from the Classical adverbial accusative بُكْرَةً (bukratan, 'early in the morning, at daybreak'), root ب-ك-ر (b-k-r).

بكى.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *bakay- ('to weep, cry'), yielding Classical Arabic بَكَى (bakā), root ب-ك-ي (b-k-y).

بكير.etymology: Signature Levantine adverb بِكِّير (bikkīr, 'early'), an intensive formation on the pattern فِعِّيل from the root ب-ك-ر (b-k-r, 'early morning, setting out at dawn').

بلا.etymology: Compound preposition بِلَا (bilā, 'without; let\'s skip / no...'), formed from the proclitic preposition بِـ (bi-) + negative particle لَا (lā).

بلد.etymology: Classical Arabic بَلَد (balad, 'town, city, settlement, country'), referring in Jordanian usage especially to downtown (وسط البلد), root ب-ل-د (b-l-d).

بلدي.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective بَلَدِيّ (baladiyy, 'local, native, home-grown, traditional') formed from بَلَد (balad, 'country, local land') + -ِيّ (-iyy).

بلدية.etymology: Feminine noun بَلَدِيَّة (baladiyya, 'municipality, city council, town hall'), coined in the 19th-century Ottoman and Arab civic reforms from بَلَدِيّ (baladiyy, 'municipal, civic').

بلوط.etymology: Classical Arabic بَلُّوط (ballūṭ, 'oak tree, acorn'), borrowed in antiquity from Aramaic בַּלּוּטָא / ܒܠܘܛܐ (ballūṭā, 'oak, acorn').

بلّش.etymology: Signature Levantine Form II verb بَلَّش (ballaš, 'to begin, start'), historically derived as a denominative from بَلَاش ('for free, from nothing/scratch') or influenced by Aramaic.

بلّغ.etymology: Form II causative verb بَلَّغَ (ballaġa, 'to cause to reach; convey a message, notify, report') from بَلَغَ (balaġa, 'to reach, attain'), root ب-ل-غ (b-l-ġ).

بناية.etymology: Verbal and concrete noun بِنَايَة (bināya, 'building, structure, edifice') from بَنَى (banā, 'to build, construct'), root ب-ن-ي (b-n-y).

بند.etymology: Classical and Modern Arabic بَنْد (band, 'clause, article of a contract, item; banner'), borrowed from Persian بَنْد (band, 'tie, joint, binding, numbered article').

بندورة.etymology: Levantine borrowing بَنْدُورَة ('tomato') from Italian pomodoro (literally pomo d'oro, 'golden apple'), adapted into Eastern Mediterranean Arabic when New World tomatoes arrived via Italian port trade in the 18th–19th centuries.

بنشر.etymology: Spoken quadriliteral verb بَنْشَر (banšar, 'to get a flat tire, break down'), denominalized from the early 20th-century automotive borrowing بَنْشَر (banšar) from English puncture.

بني.etymology: Relational (nisba) color adjective بُنِّيّ (bunniyy, 'brown, coffee-colored') derived from بُنّ (bunn, 'coffee beans, roasted coffee').

بوابة.etymology: Augmented feminine noun بَوَّابَة ('main gate, arched portal', plural بَوَّابَات) derived on the intensive pattern فَعَّالَة from بَاب ('door', root ب-و-ب), naming a grand courtyard or street entrance larger than an ordinary room door.

بياع.etymology: Occupational noun بَيَّاع (bayyāʿ, 'seller, vendor, shopkeeper') on the intensive/agentive pattern فَعَّال from بَاعَ (bāʿa, 'to sell'), root ب-ي-ع (b-y-ʿ).

بيانو.etymology: Musical instrument loanword borrowed from Italian piano (shortened from pianoforte, 'soft-loud').

بيت.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *bayt- ('house, dwelling'), related to the verbal root ب-ي-ت ('to spend the night').
بيت.notes: The same Semitic word gave rise to the Phoenician letter name *bēt* ('house'), ancestor of Greek beta (Β). In Amman, بيت names both a family home and a traditional courtyard house.

بير.etymology: Spoken and lightened Classical form بِير (bīr, 'water well') of بِئْر (biʾr) via compensatory lengthening after loss of the glottal stop, inherited from Proto-Semitic *biʾr- ('well, cistern').

بيض.etymology: Collective noun بَيْض (bayḍ, 'eggs'; singulative بَيْضَة bayḍa), inherited from Proto-Semitic *bayḍ- ('egg; whiteness'), root ب-ي-ض (b-y-ḍ).

بيع.etymology: Form I verbal noun بَيْع (bayʿ, 'selling, sale') from بَاعَ (bāʿa, 'to sell'), root ب-ي-ع (b-y-ʿ).

بين.etymology: Locative preposition بَيْنَ (bayna, 'between, among'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *bayn- ('interval, space between'), root ب-ي-ن (b-y-n).

بيّن.etymology: Form II verb بَيَّنَ (bayyana, 'to make clear, show; [in Levantine] to appear, seem, show off') from بَانَ (bāna, 'to become clear, apparent'), root ب-ي-ن (b-y-n).

بَعَد.etymology: Form I verb بَعَدَ / بَعُدَ (baʿada, 'to step back, move away, become distant') from the Semitic spatial root ب-ع-د (b-ʿ-d, 'distance, remoteness').

history.meaning: to be distant; move away; step back

بُعد.etymology: Verbal/abstract noun بُعْد (buʿd, 'distance, remoteness, dimension') on the pattern فُعْل from the root ب-ع-د (b-ʿ-d).

تأخّر.etymology: Form V reflexive verb تَأَخَّرَ (taʾaḫḫara, 'to fall behind, be delayed, be late') from أَخَّرَ (ʾaḫḫara, 'to delay, put back'), root ء-خ-ر (ʾ-ḫ-r).

history.meaning: to lag behind; be delayed; be late

تأكّد.etymology: Form V reflexive verb تَأَكَّدَ (taʾakkada, 'to become certain, make sure, verify') from أَكَّدَ (ʾakkada, 'to confirm, assure'), root ء-ك-د (ʾ-k-d).

history.meaning: to become certain; verify; make sure

تابلت.etymology: Modern digital loanword borrowed from English tablet ('portable touchscreen tablet computer').

تارت.etymology: Culinary loanword borrowed from French tarte / English tart ('open shortcrust pastry shell filled with fruit or custard').

تاريخ.etymology: Verbal noun (تَفْعِيل) of Form II أَرَّخَ (ʾarraḫa, 'to date a letter or chronicle'), linked to the Semitic moon/month word *warḫ- (compare Hebrew yārēaḥ 'moon', yereḥ 'month'): fixing an event by month and day.

تاسع.etymology: Ordinal adjective تَاسِع (tāsiʿ, 'ninth') formed on the active-participle pattern فَاعِل from تِسْعَة (tisʿa, 'nine'), root ت-س-ع (t-s-ʿ).

تاكسي.etymology: International loanword borrowed from French/English taxi (shortened from taximètre, 'taximeter cab').

تالت.etymology: Spoken Levantine reflex (with regular shift of interdental ث ṯ to stop ت t) of Classical ordinal ثَالِث (ṯāliṯ, 'third') on the pattern فَاعِل from ثَلَاثَة ('three'), root ث-ل-ث.

تاني.etymology: Spoken Levantine reflex (with regular shift of ث ṯ to ت t) of Classical ثَانٍ / الثَّانِي (ṯānī, 'second; another, other') on the ordinal pattern فَاعِل from root ث-ن-ي (ṯ-n-y, 'two; doubling').

تبدّل.etymology: Form V mediopassive verb تَبَدَّلَ (tabaddala, 'to be exchanged, get swapped, change') from بَدَّلَ (baddala, 'to change, replace'), root ب-د-ل (b-d-l).

history.meaning: to be replaced; get swapped; change

تبع.etymology: Spoken Levantine analytic possessive particle تَبَع (tabaʿ, 'belonging to, of'), grammaticalized from the Classical noun تَبَع (tabaʿ, 'follower, dependent, appurtenance'), root ت-ب-ع (t-b-ʿ, 'to follow').

تبلّل.etymology: Form V mediopassive verb تَبَلَّلَ (taballala, 'to get wet, become soaked') from بَلَّلَ (ballala, 'to wet, moisten'), root ب-ل-ل (b-l-l).

history.meaning: to become wet; get damp or soaked

تجاري.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective تِجَارِيّ (tijāriyy, 'commercial, mercantile, trade-') from تِجَارَة (tijāra, 'commerce, trade'), root ت-ج-ر (t-j-r).

تجربة.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَجْرِبَة (tajriba, 'trial, test, experiment, experience') from جَرَّبَ (jarraba, 'to test, try out'), root ج-ر-ب (j-r-b).

تحت.etymology: Locative preposition and adverb تَحْتَ (taḥta, 'under, below, beneath; downstairs'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *taḥt- ('under, below'), root ت-ح-ت.

تحتاني.etymology: Levantine relational adjective تَحْتَانِيّ (taḥtānī, 'bottom, lower, downstairs'), formed from تَحْت (taḥt, 'under, below') with the augmented relational suffix -َانِيّ (-ānī, shared with Aramaic -ānāyā).

تحرّك.etymology: Form V mediopassive verb تَحَرَّكَ (taḥarraka, 'to move, stir, shift') from حَرَّكَ (ḥarraka, 'to set in motion, move'), root ح-ر-ك (ḥ-r-k).

history.meaning: to move (intransitive); be set in motion

تحويل.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَحْوِيل (taḥwīl, 'turning, conversion, transfer, diversion') from حَوَّلَ (ḥawwala, 'to transform, transfer'), root ح-و-ل (ḥ-w-l).

تحية.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَحِيَّة (taḥiyya, 'greeting, salutation, salute, toast') from حَيَّا (ḥayyā, originally 'to say حَيَّاكَ اللّٰهُ [may God preserve your life]'), root ح-ي-ي (ḥ-y-y, 'life').

تخانق.etymology: Form VI reciprocal verb تَخَانَقَ (taḫānaqa, 'to quarrel, argue heatedly'), literally 'to seize one another by the throat', from خَنَقَ (ḫanaqa, 'to throttle, choke'), root خ-ن-ق (ḫ-n-q).

تخبّى.etymology: Spoken Levantine Form V reflexive verb تَخَبَّى (tḫabbā, 'to hide oneself, take cover'), from Classical تَخَبَّأَ (taḫabbaʾa) with regular loss of final hamza, root خ-ب-ء (ḫ-b-ʾ).

تخت.etymology: Everyday Levantine noun تَخْت (taḫt, 'bed, bedstead; raised platform'), borrowed from Persian تَخْت (taxt, 'throne, raised wooden platform, couch, bedstead').

تخيّل.etymology: Form V verb تَخَيَّلَ (taḫayyala, 'to imagine, fancy, picture in the mind') from خَيَال (ḫayāl, 'image, vision, imagination'), root خ-ي-ل (ḫ-y-l).

تدفئة.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَدْفِئَة (tadfiʾa, 'warming, heating') from دَفَّأَ (daffaʾa, 'to make warm, heat'), root د-ف-ء (d-f-ʾ, 'warmth').

تذكرة.etymology: Verbal noun of Form II ذَكَّرَ ('to remind'), built on the root ذ-ك-ر ('remember, mention') with the pattern تَفْعِلَة: originally 'a written reminder or memorandum', whence Ottoman and modern Arabic specialized it to a travel or admission 'ticket'.

تذكّر.etymology: Form V verb تَذَكَّرَ (taḏakkara, 'to remember, recall, bear in mind') from ذَكَّرَ (ḏakkara, 'to remind'), derived from the Proto-Semitic root ذ-ك-ر (*ḏ-k-r, 'to remember, mention').

تراث.etymology: Classical Arabic تُرَاث (turāṯ, 'heritage, inheritance'), formed with regular initial w -> t assimilation (*wurāṯ > turāṯ) from root و-ر-ث (w-r-ṯ, 'to inherit').

تراثي.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective تُرَاثِيّ (turāṯiyy, 'heritage, traditional, historic') from تُرَاث (turāṯ < *wurāṯ, 'inheritance, cultural heritage'), from وَرِثَ ('to inherit', root و-ر-ث).

ترتيب.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَرْتِيب (tartīb, 'putting in order, arrangement, tidiness') from رَتَّبَ (rattaba, 'to arrange, order, tidy'), root ر-ت-ب (r-t-b).

ترقّى.etymology: Form V verb تَرَقَّى (taraqqā, 'to ascend step by step, advance, get promoted') from رَقِيَ (raqiya, 'to climb, ascend'), root ر-ق-ي (r-q-y).

history.meaning: to rise by degrees; be promoted

ترك.etymology: Form I verb تَرَكَ (taraka, 'to leave, let be, leave behind'), root ت-ر-ك (t-r-k).

history.meaning: to leave; let alone; leave behind

تسعة.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *tišʿ- ('nine'), yielding Classical Arabic تِسْعَة (tisʿa), root ت-س-ع (t-s-ʿ).

تسعطعشر.etymology: Spoken Levantine construct compound numeral تِسَعْطَعْشَر (tisaʿṭaʿšar, 'nineteen' before a counted noun), contracted from Classical تِسْعَةَ عَشَرَ (tisʿata ʿašara, 'nine-teen') with pharyngeal-induced emphasis of t to ṭ.

تشرّف.etymology: Form V verb تَشَرَّفَ (tašarrafa, 'to be honored; [in تَشَرَّفْنَا] we are honored / pleased to meet you') from شَرَّفَ (šarrafa, 'to honor'), root ش-ر-ف (š-r-f, 'elevation, nobility, honor').

تصالح.etymology: Form VI reciprocal verb تَصَالَحَ (taṣālaḥa, 'to make peace with one another, reconcile') from صُلْح (ṣulḥ, 'peace, reconciliation'), root ص-ل-ح (ṣ-l-ḥ).

تطلع.etymology: Spoken Levantine Form V verb تْطَلَّع (tṭallaʿ, 'to look at, gaze upon'), from Classical تَطَلَّعَ (taṭallaʿa, 'to crane the neck to look, gaze toward'), root ط-ل-ع (ṭ-l-ʿ).

history.meaning: to look out toward; gaze closely

تطور.etymology: Form V verbal noun تَطَوُّر (taṭawwur, 'development, progress, stage-by-stage evolution') from تَطَوَّرَ (taṭawwara, 'to develop through successive stages [أَطْوَار]'), root ط-و-ر (ṭ-w-r).

تعال.etymology: Suppletive imperative verb تَعَالَ (taʿāla, f. تَعَالَيْ, pl. تَعَالَوْا, 'come!'), originally the Form VI imperative of عَلَا (ʿalā, 'to rise, ascend'), meaning literally 'come up here!', root ع-ل-و (ʿ-l-w).

تعديل.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَعْدِيل (taʿdīl, 'straightening, adjustment, modification, edit') from عَدَّلَ (ʿaddala, 'to make straight, adjust evenly'), root ع-د-ل (ʿ-d-l).

تعريشة.etymology: Form II instance/concrete noun تَعْرِيشَة (taʿrīša, 'garden trellis, vine arbor, pergola') from عَرَّشَ (ʿarraša, 'to train a vine over a wooden trellis [عَرِيش]'), root ع-ر-ش (ʿ-r-š).

تعرّف.etymology: Form V verb تَعَرَّفَ (taʿarrafa, 'to become acquainted with, get to know, meet') from عَرَفَ (ʿarafa, 'to know, recognize'), root ع-ر-ف (ʿ-r-f).

history.meaning: to get to know; become acquainted

تعلّم.etymology: Form V reflexive verb تَعَلَّمَ (taʿallama, 'to learn, study') from عَلَّمَ (ʿallama, 'to teach'), root ع-ل-م (ʿ-l-m, 'knowledge').

تعيين.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَعْيِين (taʿyīn, 'specifying, designation, appointment to a post') from عَيَّنَ (ʿayyana, 'to single out, appoint'), denominative from عَيْن ('eye; specific individual'), root ع-ي-ن.

تفاح.etymology: Collective noun تُفَّاح (tuffāḥ, 'apples'; singulative تُفَّاحَة), a Northwest/Central Semitic fruit name (cognate with Hebrew תַּפּוּחַ tappūaḥ) traditionally connected to the root ن-ف-ح / ف-و-ح ('to diffuse a sweet fragrance').

تفتيش.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَفْتِيش (taftīš, 'searching, inspection, examination') from فَتَّشَ (fattaša, 'to search carefully, inspect'), root ف-ت-ش (f-t-š).

تفرّج.etymology: Form V verb تَفَرَّجَ (tafarraja, 'to watch, look on at a view or spectacle'), originally 'to dispel worry [فَرَج] by going out to view something pleasant', from root ف-ر-ج (f-r-j, 'opening, relief from grief').

history.meaning: to find relief by viewing; watch; look on

تفضّل.etymology: Form V hospitality verb تَفَضَّلَ (tafaḍḍala, 'to be so kind as to; [imperative تَفَضَّلْ] please come in, have a seat, go ahead, here you are'), from فَضْل (faḍl, 'grace, kindness, favor'), root ف-ض-ل (f-ḍ-l).

history.meaning: to confer a favor; deign; 'please go ahead'

تفقّد.etymology: Form V verb تَفَقَّدَ (tafaqqada, 'to check on, inspect, look for what may be missing') from فَقَدَ (faqada, 'to lose, miss'), root ف-ق-د (f-q-d).

history.meaning: to seek out; inspect; check on

تفكير.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَفْكِير (tafkīr, 'thinking, thought, reflection') from فَكَّرَ (fakkara, 'to think, ponder'), root ف-ك-ر (f-k-r).

تقديم.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَقْدِيم (taqdīm, 'bringing forward, offering, serving guests, presentation') from قَدَّمَ (qaddama, 'to present, serve'), root ق-د-م (q-d-m).

تقدّم.etymology: Form V reflexive/mediopassive verb تَقَدَّمَ (taqaddama, 'to step forward, advance, progress; be served') from قَدَّمَ (qaddama, 'to bring forward, serve'), root ق-د-م (q-d-m).

history.meaning: to step forward; advance; be served

تقيل.etymology: Spoken Levantine reflex (with regular shift of interdental ث ṯ to stop ت t) of Classical Arabic ثَقِيل (ṯaqīl, 'heavy, weighty') on the pattern فَعِيل from ثَقُلَ (ṯaqula, 'to be heavy'), root ث-ق-ل.

تقييم.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَقْيِيم (taqyīm, 'valuation, assessment, rating, review') from قَيَّمَ (qayyama, 'to evaluate, appraise'), denominative from قِيمَة (qīma, 'value, worth'), root ق-و-م (q-w-m).

تلاتة.etymology: Spoken Levantine reflex (with regular shift of interdental ث ṯ to stop ت t) of Classical ثَلَاثَة (ṯalāṯa, 'three'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *śalāṯ- ('three'), root ث-ل-ث.

تلاتين.etymology: Spoken Levantine reflex (with regular shift of ث ṯ to ت t) of Classical ثَلَاثُونَ / ثَلَاثِينَ (ṯalāṯīna, 'thirty'), decade numeral formed from ثَلَاث ('three'), root ث-ل-ث.

تلاجة.etymology: Spoken Levantine reflex (with shift of ث ṯ to ت t) of ثَلَّاجَة (ṯallāja, 'icebox, refrigerator'), an instrumental/appliance noun on the pattern فَعَّالَة derived from ثَلْج (ṯalj, 'snow, ice'), root ث-ل-ج.

تلة.etymology: Singulative noun تَلَّة ('a hill') from collective تَلّ ('mound, hillock'), rooted in ت-ل-ل and shared across ancient Mesopotamian and Levantine topography (familiar in archaeology as 'tell', a layered settlement mound).

cognates.meaning: Middle Eastern archaeological mound, borrowed from Arabic تَلّ

تلت.etymology: Spoken Levantine reflex (with shift of ث ṯ to ت t) of Classical ثُلْث (ṯulṯ, 'one-third; twenty minutes of an hour'), formed on the fractional pattern فُعْل from the numeral root ث-ل-ث ('three').

تلج.etymology: Levantine pronunciation تَلْج (talj, 'ice; snow') of Classical Arabic ثَلْج (ṯalj), inherited from Proto-Semitic `*ṯalg-` ('snow,winter ice') with regular urban Levantine shift of interdental ث (ṯ) to ت (t).

تلميع.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَلْمِيع (talmīʿ, 'polishing, buffing, making shine') from لَمَّعَ (lammaʿa, 'to polish, burnish'), from لَمَعَ ('to shine, gleam'), root ل-م-ع (l-m-ʿ).

تليفون.etymology: Modern international loanword borrowed via French téléphone / English telephone (coined from Greek τῆλε 'far' + φωνή 'voice, sound').

history.meaning: apparatus for transmitting speech over distance

تم.etymology: Everyday Levantine noun تُمّ / تِمّ (tumm / timm, 'mouth, opening, spout'), evolved in Syro-Levantine Arabic from Classical فَم (fam, 'mouth') via labial assimilation or merger with ثُمّ ('orifice, mouth').

تمام.etymology: Verbal/abstract noun تَمَام (tamām, 'completeness, perfection; [in spoken Arabic] fine, all set, spot-on!') from تَمَّ (tamma, 'to be complete, finished'), root ت-م-م (t-m-m).

تماما.etymology: Adverbial accusative تَمَامًا (tamāman, 'completely, exactly, perfectly') of تَمَام (tamām, 'completeness'), from تَمَّ ('to be complete'), root ت-م-م (t-m-m).

تمانية.etymology: Spoken Levantine reflex (with regular shift of interdental ث ṯ to stop ت t) of Classical ثَمَانِيَة (ṯamāniya, 'eight'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ṯamāniy- ('eight'), root ث-م-ن.

تمانين.etymology: Spoken Levantine reflex (with shift of ث ṯ to ت t) of Classical ثَمَانُونَ / ثَمَانِينَ (ṯamānīna, 'eighty'), decade numeral formed from ثَمَانٍ ('eight'), root ث-م-ن.

تمرن.etymology: Form V reflexive verb تَمَرَّنَ (tamarrana, 'to practice, train, exercise') from مَرَّنَ (marrana, 'to accustom, train, make supple'), root م-ر-ن (m-r-n).

تمنّى.etymology: Form V verb تَمَنَّى (tamannā, 'to wish, desire, hope for') derived from مُنْيَة (munya, 'wish, desire'), root م-ن-ي (m-n-y).

تنفّس.etymology: Form V verb تَنَفَّسَ (tanaffasa, 'to breathe, draw breath') from نَفَس (nafas, 'breath'), inherited from the Proto-Semitic root ن-ف-س (*n-p-š, 'breath, soul, life').

تنين.etymology: Spoken Levantine numeral تْنِين (tnēn, 'two'), evolved from Classical اِثْنَيْنِ (iṯnayn, 'two') via shift of interdental ṯ to stop t and loss of the prosthetic initial vowel, root ث-ن-ي.

توأم.etymology: Classical Arabic تَوْأَم (tawʾam, 'twin'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *tawʾam- ('twin'), root ت-ء-م / و-ء-م.

توتّر.etymology: Form V verb تَوَتَّرَ (tawattara, 'to become taut, strained; get nervous, tense up'), denominative from وَتَر (watar, 'bowstring, lute string, tendon'), root و-ت-ر (w-t-r).

history.meaning: to be stretched taut like a string; become tense

توست.etymology: Modern culinary loanword borrowed from English toast ('sliced bread browned by radiant heat').

توصيل.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَوْصِيل (tawṣīl, 'delivering, conveying, connecting') from وَصَّلَ (waṣṣala, 'to deliver, connect'), root و-ص-ل (w-ṣ-l).

توفيق.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَوْفِيق (tawfīq, 'granting success, harmonious alignment, good fortune') from وَفَّقَ (waffaqa, 'to make successful, reconcile'), root و-ف-ق (w-f-q).

توفّى.etymology: Form V verb تَوَفَّى (tawaffā, passive تُوُفِّيَ > spoken Levantine توفى twaffā, 'to pass away, die'), originally meaning 'to receive one\'s full allotted span of life', from وَفَى ('to be complete, fulfill'), root و-ف-ي (w-f-y).

history.meaning: to fulfill one's allotted span; pass away

توقيع.etymology: Form II verbal noun تَوْقِيع (tawqīʿ, 'signature, endorsement; setting down a seal or mark') from وَقَّعَ (waqqaʿa, 'to sign, register'), root و-ق-ع (w-q-ʿ).

history.meaning: affixing a seal or mark; signature

تيتا.etymology: Affectionate Levantine kinship noun تِيتَا (tētā, 'grandma, grandmother'), formed by nursery reduplication in child speech.

ثابت.etymology: Active participle adjective ثَابِت (ṯābit, 'firm, steady, fixed, stable') from ثَبَتَ (ṯabata, 'to stand firm'), root ث-ب-ت (ṯ-b-t).

ثانية.etymology: Feminine ordinal noun ثَانِيَة (ṯāniya, 'second [of time or angle]'), elliptical for القسمة الثانية ('the second subdivision [of the hour after the minute]'), from ثَانٍ ('second', root ث-ن-ي).

ثبت.etymology: Form I verb ثَبَتَ (ṯabata, 'to stand firm, hold still, remain steady') from the Semitic root ث-ب-ت (ṯ-b-t, 'firmness, steadfastness').

ثبّت.etymology: Form II causative verb ثَبَّتَ (ṯabbata, 'to fasten, fix firmly in place, stabilize') from ثَبَتَ (ṯabata, 'to stand firm'), root ث-ب-ت (ṯ-b-t).

history.meaning: to fasten; fix firmly in place

جاب.etymology: Spoken Arabic hollow verb جَاب (jāb, 'to bring'), formed by univerbation and contraction of Classical Arabic جَاءَ بِـ (jāʾa bi-, 'to come with -> to bring'), from root ج-ي-ء + preposition بِـ.

جار.etymology: Classical Arabic جَار (jār, 'neighbor, one living next door under mutual protection'), from the root ج-و-ر (j-w-r, 'proximity, neighborhood, sanctuary').

جاف.etymology: Active participle adjective جَافّ (jāff, 'dry, arid') from the geminate verb جَفَّ (jaffa, 'to become dry'), root ج-ف-ف (j-f-f).

جاكيت.etymology: Clothing loanword borrowed from French jaquette / English jacket.

جامد.etymology: Active participle adjective جَامِد (jāmid, 'solid, firm, stiff, frozen') from جَمَدَ (jamada, 'to congeal, solidify, freeze'), root ج-م-د (j-m-d).

جانبي.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective جَانِبِيّ (jānibiyy, 'side, lateral') derived from جَانِب (jānib, 'side, flank'), root ج-ن-ب (j-n-b).

جاهز.etymology: Active participle adjective جَاهِز (jāhiz, 'ready, prepared, equipped') from the root ج-ه-ز (j-h-z, 'fitting out, preparing').

جاي.etymology: Spoken Levantine active participle جَاي (jāy, 'coming, arriving; next [week/time]'), from Classical جَاءٍ (jāʾin), active participle of جَاءَ (jāʾa, 'to come'), root ج-ي-ء.

جبان.etymology: Adjective جَبَان (jabān, 'cowardly, timid, faint-hearted') on the pattern فَعَال from جَبُنَ (jabuna, 'to be timid, shrink back'), root ج-ب-ن (j-b-n).

جبل.etymology: Inherited Semitic noun جَبَل ('mountain') from the triliteral root ج-ب-ل ('to form, mould, rise as a massif'). In Amman, جبل also designates the city's historic neighbourhoods perched across rolling limestone hills (such as Jabal Amman and Jabal al-Weibdeh).

جبلي.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective جَبَلِيّ (jabaliyy, 'mountain-, mountainous, highland') derived from جَبَل (jabal, 'mountain'), root ج-ب-ل (j-b-l).

جبنة.etymology: Singulative and mass noun جُبْنَة (jubna, 'cheese') from Classical collective جُبْن (jubn, 'cheese'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *gubn- ('curdled milk, cheese'), root ج-ب-ن (j-b-n, 'to curdle, coagulate').

جبين.etymology: Inherited Semitic body-part noun جَبِين ('forehead, brow') on the pattern فَعِيل from the root ج-ب-ن, originally denoting the prominent upper brow ridge on either side of the forehead.

جد.etymology: Classical and Levantine noun covering both جَدّ (jadd, 'grandfather, ancestor') and جِدّ (jidd, 'earnestness, seriousness', as in عن جد 'seriously, really'), from the geminate Semitic root ج-د-د (j-d-d).

جدول.etymology: Classical Arabic جَدْوَل (jadwal, 'little stream, irrigation rill; by extension, a ruled column in a manuscript, chart, timetable, schedule'), root ج-د-و-ل / ج-د-ل.

جديد.etymology: Adjective جَدِيد (jadīd, 'new, fresh, recent') on the pattern فَعِيل from جَدَّ (jadda, 'to be new'), root ج-د-د (j-d-d).

جرس.etymology: Classical Arabic جَرَس (jaras, 'bell, chime'), originally denoting a low ringing sound or chime, from the root ج-ر-س (j-r-s).

جريء.etymology: Adjective جَرِيء (jarīʾ, 'bold, daring, outspoken') on the pattern فَعِيل from جَرُؤَ (jaruʾa, 'to be bold, dare'), root ج-ر-ء (j-r-ʾ).

جريدة.etymology: Originally Classical Arabic جَرِيدَة (jarīda, 'stripped palm-branch stalk' used as a writing tally or dispatch roll), from root ج-ر-د ('to strip leaves/bark'); adopted in the 19th century for 'newspaper'.

جرّب.etymology: Form II verb جَرَّبَ (jarraba, 'to test, try out, try on, experiment') from the root ج-ر-ب (j-r-b, 'putting to the test').

جزء.etymology: Classical Arabic جُزْء (juzʾ, 'part, piece, portion, section') from جَزَأَ (jazaʾa, 'to divide into parts'), root ج-ز-ء (j-z-ʾ).

جزر.etymology: Collective noun جَزَر ('carrots', singulative جَزَرَة), borrowed in early Islamic agricultural trade from Middle Persian gazar (modern Persian گزر gazar) when purple, yellow, and orange root carrots spread westward from the Iranian plateau across the Levant.

جسر.etymology: Classical Arabic جِسْر (jisr, 'bridge, causeway, beam'), shared with Aramaic גִּשְׁרָא (gišrā) and Akkadian gišru ('log bridge, beam'), root ج-س-ر (j-s-r).

جفاف.etymology: Abstract/verbal noun جَفَاف (jafāf, 'dryness, aridity, drought') on the pattern فَعَال from جَفَّ (jaffa, 'to become dry'), root ج-ف-ف (j-f-f).

جلد.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *gild- ('skin, hide, leather'), yielding Classical Arabic جِلْد (jild), root ج-ل-د (j-l-d).

جلدة.etymology: Singulative noun جِلْدَة (jilda, 'a piece of leather or hide; in craftsmanship, a leather, felt, or rubber washer/bushing') from جِلْد (jild, 'leather, skin'), root ج-ل-د.

جماعة.etymology: Collective/abstract noun جَمَاعَة (jamāʿa, 'group, company, community; [in يا جماعة] folks, everyone!') from جَمَعَ (jamaʿa, 'to gather, bring together'), root ج-م-ع (j-m-ʿ).

جمال.etymology: Abstract noun جَمَال (jamāl, 'beauty, grace, comeliness') from جَمُلَ (jamula, 'to be beautiful, handsome'), root ج-م-ل (j-m-l).

جمع.etymology: Form I verb جَمَعَ (jamaʿa, 'to gather, collect, bring together, add') from the Semitic root ج-م-ع (j-m-ʿ, 'gathering, uniting').

جمعة.etymology: From the root ج-م-ع (j-m-', 'to gather, bring together'), naming Friday (يوم الجمعة) as the day of congregational gathering.
جمعة.notes: Unlike the earlier days of the week counted numerically from Sunday through Thursday, Friday takes its name from community assembly.

جملة.etymology: Noun جُمْلَة (jumla, 'sum, aggregate, whole; grammatical sentence or clause') from جَمَلَ (jamala, 'to gather into a whole, sum up'), root ج-م-ل (j-m-l).

جنب.etymology: Noun and locative preposition جَنْب (janb, 'side, flank; beside, next to'), inherited from the Semitic root ج-ن-ب (j-n-b, 'side').

جنوب.etymology: Classical Arabic جَنُوب (janūb, 'south; south wind'), derived from the root ج-ن-ب (j-n-b, 'side, quarter of the sky').

جنينة.etymology: Diminutive of جَنَّة (janna, 'garden, orchard'), from the triliteral root ج-ن-ن (j-n-n) expressing covering and dense foliage shading the ground. Standard Levantine word for a courtyard or home garden.

جهة.etymology: Noun جِهَة (jiha < *wijha, 'side, direction, facing quarter'), formed with regular loss of root-initial w- from وَجْه (wajh, 'face, front'), root و-ج-ه (w-j-h).

جهّز.etymology: Form II verb جَهَّزَ (jahhaza, 'to prepare, equip, make ready'), denominative from جَهَاز (jahāz, 'equipment, outfit, gear'), root ج-ه-ز (j-h-z).

جوا.etymology: Spoken Levantine adverb and preposition جُوَّا (juwwā, 'inside, indoors, within'), from Classical جَوًّا (from جَوّ 'interior of a house, midst') reinforced by Aramaic גַּוָּא / ܓܘܐ (gawwā, 'interior, inside'), root ج-و-و.

جوز.etymology: Classical Arabic collective noun جَوْز ('walnuts; walnut timber'), borrowed early from Middle Persian gōz ('walnut') and prized across Damascus and Amman for fine inlaid furniture and piano cabinetry (خشب جوز).

cognates.meaning: walnut, from the same Iranian source

جوعان.etymology: Adjective جَوْعَان (jawʿān > Levantine جوعان jūʿān, 'hungry') on the bodily-state pattern فَعْلَان from جَاعَ (jāʿa, 'to feel hunger'), root ج-و-ع (j-w-ʿ).

جيبة.etymology: Levantine singulative noun جَيْبَة (jēbe, 'pocket') from Classical جَيْب (jayb, 'bosom opening of a garment, pocket'), root ج-ي-ب (j-y-b).

حاجب.etymology: Active participle noun حَاجِب (ḥājib, 'eyebrow; screen, chamberlain'), literally 'that which screens or shades the eye', from حَجَبَ (ḥajaba, 'to veil, screen, shield'), root ح-ج-ب (ḥ-j-b).

حارة.etymology: Urban noun حَارَة (ḥāra, 'neighborhood, residential quarter, lane, alley'), derived from the root ح-و-ر / ح-ي-ر ('enclosed quarter, cluster of dwellings').

history.meaning: quarter of a city; neighborhood; lane

حاسس.etymology: Spoken Levantine active participle حَاسِس (ḥāsis, 'feeling, sensing'), formed with regular dialectal uncontracted geminate stem from Classical حَاسّ (ḥāss), active participle of حَسَّ (ḥassa, 'to feel'), root ح-س-س.

حاطط.etymology: Spoken Levantine active participle حَاطِط (ḥāṭiṭ, 'putting, having placed or packed'), formed with uncontracted geminate stem from Classical حَاطّ (ḥāṭṭ), active participle of حَطَّ (ḥaṭṭa, 'to put, set down'), root ح-ط-ط.

حال.etymology: Classical Arabic حَال (ḥāl, 'condition, state, circumstance; [in Levantine with pronoun suffixes] oneself') from حَالَ (ḥāla, 'to turn, shift, change state'), root ح-و-ل (ḥ-w-l).

حاليا.etymology: Adverbial accusative حَالِيًّا (ḥāliyyan, 'at present, currently, for now') from the relational adjective حَالِيّ (ḥāliyy, 'present, current'), derived from حَال ('present state', root ح-و-ل).

حامل.etymology: Active participle noun حَامِل (ḥāmil, 'carrier, bearer; music stand, holder, rack') from حَمَلَ (ḥamala, 'to carry, bear, hold up'), root ح-م-ل (ḥ-m-l).

حاول.etymology: Form III verb حَاوَلَ (ḥāwala, 'to try, attempt, endeavor') from the root ح-و-ل (ḥ-w-l, 'shifting, seeking a way or means [حِيلَة]').

history.meaning: to seek a way; attempt; try

حب.etymology: Form I (and Classical Form IV أَحَبَّ) geminate verb حَبَّ (ḥabba, 'to love, like, hold dear'), inherited from the Proto-Semitic root ح-ب-ب (*ḥ-b-b, 'to love, cherish').

حبة.etymology: Singulative noun حَبَّة (ḥabba, 'a single grain, seed, berry, pill; a single piece or item') from collective حَبّ (ḥabb, 'grain, seed, kernels'), root ح-ب-ب (ḥ-b-b).

حبر.etymology: Classical Arabic حِبْر (ḥibr, 'ink; beauty, fine mark'), from Semitic root ح-ب-ر (ḥ-b-r, 'to adorn, stripe, write finely with ink').

حبيب.etymology: Adjective and affectionate noun حَبِيب (ḥabīb, 'beloved, dear, darling') on the pattern فَعِيل from حَبَّ (ḥabba, 'to love'), root ح-ب-ب (ḥ-b-b).

حتى.etymology: Preposition, conjunction, and focus particle حَتَّى (ḥattā, 'until, up to, so that; even'), inherited from Central Semitic.

حجر.etymology: Classical Arabic حَجَر (ḥajar, 'stone, rock'), from the Semitic root ح-ج-ر (ḥ-j-r).

حجري.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective حَجَرِيّ (ḥajariyy, 'made of stone, stony') derived from حَجَر (ḥajar, 'stone') + -ِيّ (-iyy), root ح-ج-ر.

حجز.etymology: Form I verbal noun حَجْز (ḥajz, 'holding back, setting aside, booking, reservation') from حَجَزَ (ḥajaza, 'to separate, hold back, reserve'), root ح-ج-ز (ḥ-j-z).

حدا.etymology: Spoken Levantine indefinite pronoun حَدَا (ḥadā, 'someone, anyone'), evolved by loss of the initial syllable from the Classical accusative أَحَدًا (ʾaḥadan, 'anyone, someone'), from أَحَد ('one', root و-ح-د / ء-ح-د).

حدعش.etymology: Spoken Levantine compound numeral حْدَعْش (ḥdaʿš, 'eleven'), contracted from Classical أَحَدَ عَشَرَ (ʾaḥada ʿašara, 'one-teen') via aphesis of initial ʾa- and reduction of -ʿašar to -ʿš.

حديث.etymology: Adjective حَدِيث (ḥadīṯ, 'new, recent, modern') on the pattern فَعِيل from حَدَثَ (ḥadaṯa, 'to happen newly, be young/new'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ḥadaṯ- ('new'), root ح-د-ث.

حديد.etymology: From the geminate root ح-د-د (h-d-d, 'to be sharp, keen, bounded'), originally describing sharpened metal and generalized in Arabic to 'iron'.
حديد.notes: Used for gates (بوابة حديد), heavy wrenches (مفتاح حديد), and hardware.

حذاء.etymology: Classical Arabic حِذَاء ('shoe, footwear', plural أَحْذِيَة) from the root ح-ذ-و ('place sole-to-sole, cut leather to match the foot's outline'), originally naming a strapped leather sandal cut to the exact measure of its wearer.

حرارة.etymology: Abstract noun حَرَارَة (ḥarāra, 'heat, warmth, temperature') on the pattern فَعَالَة from حَرَّ (ḥarra, 'to be hot, warm'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ḥarār- ('to burn, be hot'), root ح-ر-ر.

حرام.etymology: In Levantine household usage, حْرَام (ḥrām, 'woolen bed blanket'), shortened from Classical إِحْرَام (iḥrām, 'seamless woolen wrap or cloak'); homographic with Classical حَرَام (ḥarām, 'forbidden, sacred; a pity!'), both from the Semitic root ح-ر-م (ḥ-r-m).

حرف.etymology: Classical Arabic حَرْف (ḥarf, 'sharp edge, border, rim; letter of the alphabet, grammatical particle'), from the root ح-ر-ف (ḥ-r-f, 'edge, turning aside').

history.meaning: edge; border; letter of the alphabet

حرك.etymology: Form II transitive verb حَرَّكَ (ḥarraka, 'to move, stir, set in motion, wiggle') from حَرُكَ (ḥaruka, 'to be in motion'), root ح-ر-ك (ḥ-r-k).

history.meaning: to set in motion; move; stir

حزر.etymology: Form I verb حَزَرَ (ḥazara, 'to estimate, conjecture, guess'), root ح-ز-ر (ḥ-z-r).

حس.etymology: Form I (and Form IV أَحَسَّ) geminate verb حَسَّ (ḥassa, 'to feel, sense, perceive'), from the Semitic root ح-س-س (ḥ-s-s, 'feeling, perception, faint sound').

حساب.etymology: Verbal and concrete noun حِسَاب (ḥisāb, 'reckoning, calculation, bill, account') from حَسَبَ (ḥasaba, 'to count, reckon, compute'), root ح-س-ب (ḥ-s-b).

حضرتك.etymology: Polite second-person honorific pronoun حَضْرَتُكَ (ḥaḍratuka > Levantine ḥaḍritak [m.] / ḥaḍirtik [f.], 'you, sir/ma\'am'), literally 'your presence', from حَضْرَة (ḥaḍra, 'presence, dignity', root ح-ض-ر) + possessive suffix -كَ (-ka).

حط.etymology: Form I geminate verb حَطَّ (ḥaṭṭa, 'to put down, place, set, lower'), from the root ح-ط-ط (ḥ-ṭ-ṭ).

حفر.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ḥapar- ('to dig, excavate'), yielding Classical Arabic حَفَرَ (ḥafara, 'to dig, carve, wear a groove in'), root ح-ف-ر (ḥ-f-r).

حفظ.etymology: Form I verbal noun حِفْظ (ḥifẓ, 'safekeeping, preservation, guarding, learning by heart') from حَفِظَ (ḥafiẓa, 'to guard, keep safe, preserve'), root ح-ف-ظ (ḥ-f-ẓ).

حفلة.etymology: Instance and concrete noun حَفْلَة (ḥafla, 'gathering, celebration, party, concert') from حَفَلَ (ḥafala, 'to gather in a crowd, assemble'), root ح-ف-ل (ḥ-f-l).

حفيد.etymology: Kinship noun حَفِيد (ḥafīd, 'grandson, grandchild') on the pattern فَعِيل from حَفَدَ (ḥafada, 'to walk briskly in service, attend upon elders in the household'), root ح-ف-د (ḥ-f-d).

حق.etymology: Classical Arabic حَقّ (ḥaqq, 'truth, right, just claim, due price') from حَقَّ (ḥaqqa, 'to be true, right, binding'), from the Proto-Semitic root ح-ق-ق (*ḥ-q-q, 'to cut/inscribe a law, be rightful').

حقيقة.etymology: Feminine noun حَقِيقَة (ḥaqīqa, 'truth, reality, fact') on the pattern فَعِيلَة from حَقَّ (ḥaqqa, 'to be true, real, established'), root ح-ق-ق (ḥ-q-q).

حقيقي.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective حَقِيقِيّ (ḥaqīqiyy, 'real, true, genuine, authentic') derived from حَقِيقَة (ḥaqīqa, 'truth, reality'), root ح-ق-ق.

حك.etymology: Form I geminate verb حَكَّ (ḥakka, 'to rub, scrape, scratch; itch'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ḥakak- ('to scratch, rub'), root ح-ك-ك (ḥ-k-k).

حكى.etymology: Form I verb حَكَى (ḥakā, 'to relate, recount, narrate; [in Levantine] to speak, talk, tell'), from the root ح-ك-ي (ḥ-k-y).

حكي.etymology: Verbal noun حَكْي (ḥaky > Levantine حَكِي ḥakī, 'talk, speech, words') from حَكَى (ḥakā, 'to speak, tell'), root ح-ك-ي (ḥ-k-y).

حكيم.etymology: Adjective حَكِيم (ḥakīm, 'wise, judicious, sensible; sage') on the pattern فَعِيل from حَكُمَ (ḥakuma, 'to be wise, exercise sound judgment'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ḥakam- ('to be wise'), root ح-ك-م.

حلقة.etymology: Noun حَلْقَة / حَلَقَة (ḥalqa, 'ring, circular link, metal washer; circle of people; series episode') from the root ح-ل-ق (ḥ-l-q, 'circle, ring').

حلم.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ḥulm- ('dream, vision in sleep'), yielding Classical Arabic حُلْم (ḥulm), root ح-ل-م (ḥ-l-m).

حلو.etymology: Adjective حُلْو (ḥulw > Levantine ḥilw / ḥilu, 'sweet, pleasant, lovely, nice, pretty') from حَلَا (ḥalā, 'to be sweet, pleasing'), root ح-ل-و (ḥ-l-w).

حليب.etymology: From the Proto-Semitic dairy root ح-ل-ب (*ḥ-l-b, 'to milk'), formed on the pattern فَعيل ('freshly milked milk').
حليب.notes: Whereas Classical لبن meant fresh milk, in Levantine Arabic حليب means fresh milk while لبن denotes yoghurt.

حمام.etymology: Noun حَمَّام (ḥammām, 'bath, bathhouse, bathroom') on the pattern فَعَّال from the Proto-Semitic root ح-م-م (*ḥ-m-m, 'to be hot, heat water').

حماية.etymology: Form I verbal noun حِمَايَة (ḥimāya, 'protection, safeguarding, defense') from حَمَى (ḥamā, 'to protect, guard, defend'), root ح-م-ي (ḥ-m-y).

حمد.etymology: Form I verbal noun حَمْد (ḥamd, 'praise, commendation, thankfulness', as in الحَمْدُ لِلّٰهِ 'praise be to God / thank goodness') from حَمِدَ (ḥamida, 'to praise, thank'), root ح-م-د (ḥ-m-d).

حمل.etymology: Form I verb حَمَلَ (ḥamala, 'to carry, bear, lift, hold up'), inherited from the Semitic root ح-م-ل (ḥ-m-l, 'carrying, bearing a load').

حوالين.etymology: Spoken Levantine preposition حَوَالَيْن (ḥawālēn, 'around, all around'), formed as an oblique dual/plural extension of Classical حَوَالَيْ (ḥawālay, 'around, surrounding'), from حَوْل (root ح-و-ل, 'going around, circuit').

حوّل.etymology: Form II causative verb حَوَّلَ (ḥawwala, 'to turn, shift, convert, transform, transfer') from حَالَ (ḥāla, 'to change state, shift'), root ح-و-ل (ḥ-w-l).

حي.etymology: Classical Arabic حَيّ (ḥayy, 'kinship group, encampment, urban quarter, neighborhood district'), derived from the Semitic root ح-ي-ي (ḥ-y-y, 'life, living community').

حياة.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ḥayy-at- ('life'), spelled in Classical orthography as حَيَوٰة / حَيَاة (ḥayāh), root ح-ي-ي (ḥ-y-y).

حيط.etymology: Spoken Levantine noun حَيْط (ḥēṭ, 'wall'; plural حِيطَان ḥīṭān), contracted from Classical حَائِط (ḥāʾiṭ, 'enclosing wall'), originally the active participle of حَاطَ (ḥāṭa, 'to surround, enclose, guard'), root ح-و-ط.

حَجَز.etymology: Form I verb حَجَزَ (ḥajaza, 'to hold back, set aside, book, reserve; vocalized to distinguish the verb from the noun حَجْز'), root ح-ج-ز (ḥ-j-z).

history.meaning: to hold back; set aside; reserve

حَيّ.etymology: Adjective حَيّ (ḥayy, 'alive, living, live; vocalized with shadda to distinguish it from the homographic noun حَيّ "quarter"'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ḥayy- ('alive, living'), root ح-ي-ي.

حِفِظ.etymology: Form I verb حَفِظَ (ḥafiẓa > Levantine حِفِظ ḥifiẓ, 'to keep safe, preserve, hold onto, memorize; vocalized to distinguish the verb from the verbal noun حِفْظ'), root ح-ف-ظ (ḥ-f-ẓ).

history.meaning: to guard; keep safe; preserve; memorize

حِلِم.etymology: Form I verb حَلَمَ (ḥalama > Levantine حِلِم ḥilim, 'to dream; vocalized to distinguish the verb from the noun حُلْم "dream"'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ḥalam- ('to dream'), root ح-ل-م.

خارجي.etymology: Relational (nisba) adjective خَارِجِيّ (ḫārijiyy, 'outer, exterior, outside') derived from خَارِج (ḫārij, 'outside, exterior', active participle of خَرَجَ 'to go out'), root خ-ر-ج (ḫ-r-j).

خاص.etymology: Active participle adjective خَاصّ (ḫāṣṣ, 'special, private, particular, exclusive') from the geminate verb خَصَّ (ḫaṣṣa, 'to single out, belong specifically to'), root خ-ص-ص (ḫ-ṣ-ṣ).

خاف.etymology: Hollow Form I stative verb خَافَ (ḫāfa < *ḫawifa, 'to fear, be afraid, worry'), from the root خ-و-ف (ḫ-w-f, 'fear, dread').

خباز.etymology: Occupational noun خَبَّاز (ḫabbāz, 'baker') on the professional pattern فَعَّال from خَبَزَ (ḫabaza, 'to bake bread'), root خ-ب-ز (ḫ-b-z).

خبر.etymology: Classical Arabic خَبَر (ḫabar, 'news, report, tidings, piece of information') from the root خ-ب-ر (ḫ-b-r, 'knowing by experience, informing').

خبز.etymology: From the triliteral root خ-ب-ز (kh-b-z, 'to bake bread'), common across Arabic and Ethiopian Semitic.
خبز.notes: Fresh morning خبز is a staple of every Jordanian breakfast table.

خبط.etymology: Form I verb خَبَطَ (ḫabaṭa, 'to strike, beat, knock or bump into'), inherited from the Semitic root خ-ب-ط (ḫ-b-ṭ, 'beating, striking').

خبّر.etymology: Form II verb خَبَّرَ (ḫabbara, 'to inform, tell, report news to someone') from خَبَر (ḫabar, 'news, report'), root خ-ب-ر (ḫ-b-r).

خبّى.etymology: Spoken Levantine Form II verb خَبَّى (ḫabbā, 'to hide, conceal, put away safely'), from Classical خَبَّأَ (ḫabbaʾa) via regular loss of final glottal stop, root خ-ب-ء (ḫ-b-ʾ).

ختم.etymology: Classical Arabic خَتْم (ḫatm, 'seal, stamp, signet impression'), from the Semitic root خ-ت-م (ḫ-t-m, 'to seal, stamp, conclude'), ultimately an ancient borrowing from Egyptian ḫtm ('seal, signet ring; to seal').

خجل.etymology: Form I stative verb خَجِلَ (ḫajila, 'to feel shy, be bashful or embarrassed'), from the root خ-ج-ل (ḫ-j-l, 'shyness, bashfulness').

history.meaning: to feel shy; be abashed or embarrassed

خدش.etymology: Form I verbal and concrete noun خَدْش (ḫadš, 'scratch, scrape, abrasion') from خَدَشَ (ḫadaša, 'to scratch, mar the surface'), root خ-د-ش (ḫ-d-š).

خدع.etymology: Form I verb خَدَعَ (ḫadaʿa, 'to deceive, trick, fool, mislead'), from the root خ-د-ع (ḫ-d-ʿ, 'concealing, deceiving').

خدم.etymology: Form I verb خَدَمَ (ḫadama, 'to serve, attend upon, work in service'), from the root خ-د-م (ḫ-d-m).

خدمة.etymology: Noun خِدْمَة (ḫidma, 'service, attendance, helpful turn') from خَدَمَ (ḫadama, 'to serve'), root خ-د-م (ḫ-d-m).

خرب.etymology: Form I stative/intransitive verb خَرِبَ (ḫariba, 'to fall into ruin; [in Levantine] to break down, stop working, spoil'), from the Proto-Semitic root خ-ر-ب (*ḫ-r-b, 'ruin, desolation').

history.meaning: to fall into ruin; break down

خردوات.etymology: Plural noun خُرْدَوَات (ḫurdawāt, 'hardware, small metal wares, sundries'), borrowed via Ottoman Turkish hırdavat from Persian خُرْدَه (xurda, 'small piece, fragment, retail item') with the Arabic feminine plural ending -āt.

history.meaning: small items; retail hardware and sundries

خريطة.etymology: Classical and Modern Arabic خَرِيطَة (ḫarīṭa, 'map, chart'), combining Classical خَرِيطَة ('leathern pouch for rolled documents', root خ-ر-ط) with Mediterranean/Greek χάρτης (khártēs, 'papyrus sheet, chart, map').

خريف.etymology: Derived on pattern فَعِيل from root خ-ر-ف (ḫ-r-f, 'to pluck ripe fruit from trees'): originally the autumn fruit-picking and harvest season.

خرّب.etymology: Form II causative verb خَرَّبَ (ḫarraba, 'to ruin, wreck, break [something]') from خَرِبَ (ḫariba, 'to break down, fall into ruin'), root خ-ر-ب (ḫ-r-b).

خزانة.etymology: Noun of place/instrument خِزَانَة (ḫizāna, 'cupboard, closet, wardrobe, cabinet; treasury') from خَزَنَ (ḫazana, 'to store, lay up for safekeeping'), root خ-ز-ن (ḫ-z-n).

خزف.etymology: Classical Arabic خَزَف (ḫazaf, 'pottery, earthenware, glazed ceramic or porcelain'), cognate with Aramaic חַסְפָּא (ḥaspā) and Akkadian ḫaṣbu ('pottery, terra cotta'), root خ-ز-ف.

خزين.etymology: Noun خَزِين (ḫazīn, 'stored provisions, pantry stock, larder') on the passive-sense pattern فَعِيل ('that which is stored away') from خَزَنَ (ḫazana, 'to store'), root خ-ز-ن (ḫ-z-n).

خشب.etymology: Native Arabic collective noun from خ-ش-ب (kh-sh-b), denoting timber and woodwork.
خشب.notes: Used directly in apposition after another noun in Jordanian Arabic to indicate material: درج خشب ('wooden stairs'), قطار خشب ('wooden train').

خصم.etymology: Verbal noun خَصْم (ḫaṣm, 'deduction, price discount; adversary') from خَصَمَ (ḫaṣama, 'to deduct from an account; contend with'), root خ-ص-م (ḫ-ṣ-m).

خصوص.etymology: Verbal noun خُصُوص (ḫuṣūṣ, 'particularity, specialness; [in بِخُصُوص] regarding, concerning') from خَصَّ (ḫaṣṣa, 'to single out, concern specifically'), root خ-ص-ص (ḫ-ṣ-ṣ).

خضار.etymology: Collective noun خُضَار (ḫuḍār, 'greens, fresh vegetables') derived from the Semitic root خ-ض-ر (ḫ-ḍ-r, 'greenness, fresh herbs and vegetation').
